{{Short description|Function space}}
In [[mathematical analysis]], '''Lorentz spaces''', introduced by [[George G. Lorentz]] in the 1950s,<ref>G. Lorentz, "Some new function spaces", ''Annals of Mathematics'' '''51''' (1950), pp. 37-55.</ref><ref>G. Lorentz, "On the theory of spaces Λ", ''Pacific Journal of Mathematics'' '''1''' (1951), pp. 411-429.</ref> are generalisations of the more familiar [[Lp space|<math>L^{p}</math> spaces]].

The Lorentz spaces are denoted by <math>L^{p,q}</math>.  Like the <math>L^{p}</math> spaces, they are characterized by a [[norm (mathematics)|norm]] (technically a [[quasinorm]]) that encodes information about the "size" of a function, just as the <math>L^{p}</math> norm does.  The two basic qualitative notions of "size" of a function are: how tall is the graph of the function, and how spread out is it.  The Lorentz norms provide tighter control over both qualities than the <math>L^{p}</math> norms, by exponentially rescaling the measure in both the range (<math>p</math>) and the domain (<math>q</math>). The Lorentz norms, like the <math>L^{p}</math> norms, are invariant under arbitrary rearrangements of the values of a function.

==Definition==
The Lorentz space on a [[measure space]] <math>(X, \mu)</math> is the space of extended-complex-valued [[measurable function]]s <math>f:X\rightarrow \mathbb{\overline{C}}</math> such that the following [[quasinorm]] is finite

:<math>\|f\|_{L^{p,q}(X,\mu)} = p^{\frac{1}{q}} \left \|t\mu\{|f|\ge t\}^{\frac{1}{p}} \right \|_{L^q \left (\mathbf{R}^+, \frac{dt}{t} \right)}
</math> 

where <math>0 < p < \infty</math> and <math>0 < q \leq \infty</math>.  Thus, when <math>q < \infty</math>,

:<math>\|f\|_{L^{p,q}(X,\mu)}=p^{\frac{1}{q}}\left(\int_0^\infty t^q \mu\left\{x : |f(x)| \ge t\right\}^{\frac{q}{p}}\,\frac{dt}{t}\right)^{\frac{1}{q}}
= \left(\int_0^\infty \bigl(\tau \mu\left\{x : |f(x)|^p \ge \tau \right\}\bigr)^{\frac{q}{p}}\,\frac{d\tau}{\tau}\right)^{\frac{1}{q}}
.</math>

and, when <math>q = \infty</math>,

:<math>\|f\|_{L^{p,\infty}(X,\mu)}^p = \sup_{t>0}\left(t^p\mu\left\{x : |f(x)| > t \right\}\right).</math>

It is also conventional to set <math>L^{\infty,\infty}(X, \mu) = L^{\infty}(X, \mu)</math>. Given that <math>L^{\infty}_{\mathrm{w}}(X, \mu) = L^{\infty}(X, \mu)</math>, we get the following chain of equalities: <math>L^{\infty,\infty}(X, \mu) = L^{\infty}_{\mathrm{w}}(X, \mu) = L^{\infty}(X, \mu)</math>. Here, <math>L^{\infty}_{\mathrm{w}}(X, \mu)</math> is the [[Lp space#Weak Lp|weak Lebesgue space]].

==Decreasing rearrangements==
The quasinorm is invariant under rearranging the values of the function <math>f</math>, essentially by definition.  In particular, given a complex-valued [[measurable function]] <math>f</math> defined on a measure space, <math>(X, \mu)</math>, its '''decreasing rearrangement''' function, <math>f^{\ast}: [0, \infty) \to [0, \infty]</math> can be defined as

:<math>f^{\ast}(t) = \inf \{\alpha \in \mathbf{R}^{+}: d_f(\alpha) \leq t\}</math>

where <math>d_{f}</math> is the so-called '''distribution function''' of <math>f</math>, given by

:<math>d_f(\alpha) = \mu(\{x \in X : |f(x)| > \alpha\}).</math>

Here, for notational convenience, <math>\inf \varnothing</math> is defined to be <math>\infty</math>.

The two functions <math>|f|</math> and <math>f^{\ast}</math> are '''equimeasurable''', meaning that

:<math> \mu \bigl( \{ x \in X : |f(x)| > \alpha\} \bigr) = \lambda \bigl( \{ t > 0 : f^{\ast}(t) > \alpha\} \bigr), \quad \alpha > 0, </math>

where <math>\lambda</math> is the [[Lebesgue measure]] on the real line. The related [[symmetric decreasing rearrangement]] function, which is also equimeasurable with <math>f</math>, would be defined on the real line by

:<math>\mathbf{R} \ni t \mapsto \tfrac{1}{2} f^{\ast}(|t|).</math>

Given these definitions, for <math>0 < p < \infty</math> and <math>0 < q \leq \infty</math>, the Lorentz quasinorms are given by

:<math>\| f \|_{L^{p, q}} = \begin{cases} 
\left( \displaystyle \int_0^{\infty} \left (t^{\frac{1}{p}} f^{\ast}(t) \right )^q \, \frac{dt}{t} \right)^{\frac{1}{q}} & q \in (0, \infty), \\
\sup\limits_{t > 0} \, t^{\frac{1}{p}}  f^{\ast}(t)   & q = \infty.
\end{cases}</math>

==Lorentz sequence spaces==
When <math>(X,\mu)=(\mathbb{N},\#)</math> (the counting measure on <math>\mathbb{N}</math>), the resulting Lorentz space is a [[sequence space]].  However, in this case it is convenient to use different notation.

===Definition===
For <math>(a_n)_{n=1}^\infty\in\mathbb{R}^\mathbb{N}</math> (or <math>\mathbb{C}^\mathbb{N}</math> in the complex case), let <math display="inline">\left\|(a_n)_{n=1}^\infty\right\|_p = \left(\sum_{n=1}^\infty|a_n|^p\right)^{1/p}</math> denote the p-norm for <math>1\leq p<\infty</math> and <math display="inline">\left\|(a_n)_{n=1}^\infty\right\|_\infty = \sup_{n\in\N}|a_n|</math> the ∞-norm. Denote by <math>\ell_p</math> the Banach space of all sequences with finite p-norm. Let <math>c_0</math> the Banach space of all sequences satisfying <math>\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n=0</math>, endowed with the ∞-norm. Denote by <math>c_{00}</math> the normed space of all sequences with only finitely many nonzero entries. These spaces all play a role in the definition of the Lorentz sequence spaces <math>d(w,p)</math> below.

Let <math>w=(w_n)_{n=1}^\infty\in c_0\setminus\ell_1</math> be a sequence of positive real numbers satisfying <math>1 = w_1 \geq w_2 \geq w_3 \geq \cdots</math>, and define the norm <math display="inline">\left\|(a_n)_{n=1}^\infty\right\|_{d(w,p)} = \sup_{\sigma\in\Pi}\left\|(a_{\sigma(n)}w_n^{1/p})_{n=1}^\infty\right\|_p</math>. The ''Lorentz sequence space'' <math>d(w,p)</math> is defined as the Banach space of all sequences where this norm is finite. Equivalently, we can define <math>d(w,p)</math> as the completion of <math>c_{00}</math> under <math>\|\cdot\|_{d(w,p)}</math>.

==Properties==
The Lorentz spaces are genuinely generalisations of the <math>L^{p}</math> spaces in the sense that, for any <math>p</math>, <math>L^{p,p} = L^{p}</math>, which follows from [[Cavalieri's principle]]. Further, <math>L^{p, \infty}</math> coincides with [[Lp space#Weak Lp|weak Lebesgue space]] <math>L^{p}_{\mathrm{w}}</math>. They are [[Quasinorm|quasi-Banach spaces]] (that is, quasi-normed spaces which are also complete) and are normable for <math>1 < p < \infty</math> and <math>1 \leq q \leq \infty</math>. When <math>p = 1</math>, <math>L^{1, 1} = L^{1}</math> is equipped with a norm, but it is not possible to define a norm equivalent to the quasinorm of <math>L^{1,\infty}</math>, the space <math>L^{1}_{\mathrm{w}}</math>.  As a concrete example that the triangle inequality fails in <math>L^{1,\infty}</math>, consider
 
:<math>f(x) = \tfrac{1}{x} \chi_{(0,1)}(x)\quad \text{and} \quad g(x) = \tfrac{1}{1-x} \chi_{(0,1)}(x),</math> 

whose <math>L^{1,\infty}</math> quasi-norm equals one, whereas the quasi-norm of their sum <math>f + g</math> equals four.

The space <math>L^{p,q}</math> is contained in <math>L^{p, r}</math> whenever <math>q < r</math>.  The Lorentz spaces are real [[interpolation space]]s between <math>L^{1}</math> and <math>L^{\infty}</math>.

===Hölder's inequality===
<math>\|fg\|_{L^{p,q}}\le A_{p_1,p_2,q_1,q_2}\|f\|_{L^{p_1,q_1}}\|g\|_{L^{p_2,q_2}}</math> where <math>0<p,p_1,p_2<\infty</math>, <math>0<q,q_1,q_2\le\infty</math>, <math>1/p=1/p_1+1/p_2</math>, and <math>1/q=1/q_1+1/q_2</math>.

===Dual space===
If <math>(X,\mu)</math> is a nonatomic σ-finite measure space, then <br />(i) <math>(L^{p,q})^*=\{0\}</math> for <math>0<p<1</math>, or <math>1=p<q<\infty</math>; <br />(ii) <math>(L^{p,q})^*=L^{p',q'}</math> for <math>1<p<\infty,0<q\le\infty</math>, or <math>0<q\le p=1</math>; <br />(iii) <math>(L^{p,\infty})^*\ne\{0\}</math> for <math>1\le p\le\infty</math>. <br />Here <math>p'=p/(p-1)</math> for <math>1<p<\infty</math>, <math>p'=\infty</math> for <math>0<p\le1</math>, and <math>\infty'=1</math>.

===Atomic decomposition===
The following are equivalent for <math>0<p\le\infty, 1\le q\le\infty</math>. <br />
(i) <math>\|f\|_{L^{p,q}}\le A_{p,q}C</math>. <br />
(ii) <math>f=\textstyle\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}f_n</math> where <math>f_n</math> has disjoint support, with measure <math>\le2^n</math>, on which <math>0<H_{n+1}\le|f_n|\le H_n</math> almost everywhere, and <math>\|H_n2^{n/p}\|_{\ell^q(\mathbb{Z})}\le A_{p,q}C</math>. <br />
(iii) <math>|f|\le\textstyle\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}H_n\chi_{E_n}</math> almost everywhere, where <math>\mu(E_n)\le A_{p,q}'2^n</math> and <math>\|H_n2^{n/p}\|_{\ell^q(\mathbb{Z})}\le A_{p,q}C</math>.<br />
(iv) <math>f=\textstyle\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}f_n</math> where <math>f_n</math> has disjoint support <math>E_n</math>, with nonzero measure, on which <math>B_02^n\le|f_n|\le B_12^n</math> almost everywhere, <math>B_0,B_1</math> are positive constants, and <math>\|2^n\mu(E_n)^{1/p}\|_{\ell^q(\mathbb{Z})}\le A_{p,q}C</math>.<br />
(v) <math>|f|\le\textstyle\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}2^n\chi_{E_n}</math> almost everywhere, where <math>\|2^n\mu(E_n)^{1/p}\|_{\ell^q(\mathbb{Z})}\le A_{p,q}C</math>.
